inline_text:
## Why

One person reaches this estate under up to three addresses — the one they typed on the form, the one Drive actually granted, and the one their Slack account carries. Collapsing those into one produced both standing confusions: *"this organizer has no Slack"* and *"this organizer is requesting access to a folder they already have."*

Both turned out to be measurement bugs, not people problems.

## The lookup bug

`users.lookupByEmail` matches on the exact string Slack stored at signup. Consumer Gmail folds dots and `+tags` into one mailbox; Slack does not. So an intake row spelled `first.last@gmail.com` missed an account registered as `firstlast@gmail.com`, and the person was reported as having no Slack at all.

`lookup_emails` now retries the canonical spelling on `users_not_found` and reports which address actually matched. Verified live against the workspace.

The fold is limited to `gmail.com`/`googlemail.com` deliberately. Dot-insensitivity is a property of *consumer Gmail*, not of Google — a Workspace account on a custom domain treats dots as significant, so folding by "looks hosted at Google" would resolve one person's row onto another person's account.

## Three identity columns on `Form Responses`

| Column | Written by | Is |
|---|---|---|
| `Slack ID` | `resolve_slack_ids.py` | the immutable `U…` id — the durable key |
| `Slack Email` | `resolve_slack_ids.py` | the address that Slack account carries |
| `Drive Email` | `track_drive_email.py` | the address actually on the chapter folder ACL |

None of them overwrites the intake `Email`: that column is what the person told us and what Drive grants are keyed to. The *difference* between the three is the fact worth being able to see.

An **id, never a handle** — a handle is a display name its owner can change, so an invite keyed off one breaks silently. Same argument `invite_organizers.py` already makes.

`(no grant)` in `Drive Email` is a visible sentinel rather than a blank, because a blank cannot be told apart from "the script has not run yet" — and the empty case is the one worth acting on.

## What is and is not decided automatically

`--write` fills only what an **email lookup** resolved. A name match is a *suggestion*, reported for review and written only via `--apply`.

That guard earned itself during this run: a `Denied` Lagos applicant shares a full name with an AAIF ops staffer, and an automatic name pass would have stamped the ops account's id onto her row. A second suggestion was held because the row's name and email belong to two different people.

Suggestions index `real_name` only. Indexing the `@handle` too made `ada.lovelace` key-match "Ada Lovelace" — a coincidence wearing a full match's confidence. Pinned by test.

## Also

- `ensure_columns` assigns indexes against a growing header width, so two new columns cannot land on the same letter and silently overwrite each other.
- Report runs no longer create their own columns — nothing changes without a write flag, matching every other engine here.

## Then the branch grew

Running the Slack audit against this work surfaced more, and a six-agent review of the result surfaced more again. All of it is on this branch.

### The audit reported our own automation as findings about people

`is_staff` tested one config value while the sheet records ops staff two other ways, so an ops admin seeded into every organizers channel by `provision_channels.py` read as an **unreviewed stranger in 87 private rooms** — ranked second in the summary that goes to leadership. It now honours the per-person `Ops staff email` list and the `Ops staff domain` list, and warns rather than staying silent when they are empty.

Two chapters can share one organizers room (Silicon Valley and San Francisco both run out of `#bay-area-organizers`), and the chapter with the empty CRM read as "a private room with nobody we vetted in it" — a finding about a room that is fully staffed. Each chapter now also reports the other's people, in a separate `shared` key: chapter questions read `accepted`, room questions read `roster(c)`. They were briefly mixed into `accepted` and filtered back out at each aggregate, which is fail-open and was already wrong for two other questions.

### An identity bug that would have invited the wrong person

`lookup_emails` looped over `gmail_variants()`, which returns `[]` for an address that strips to empty, while the caller filtered on truthiness. A cell holding only a non-breaking space — the usual artefact of a pasted spreadsheet value — ran the loop zero times, and `payload` survived from the previous iteration. That row silently inherited the **previous person's account id**, which is the id `invite_organizers` acts on.

Reproduced, fixed in both places, re-run clean. The same shape one tier down: `hydrate` swallowed every `users.info` failure, so a broken token rendered as "this person has no Slack account".

### Real PII was committed to this public repo

A real organizer's address and two real Slack ids reached `lib/` and a test fixture as "verified live" evidence. They are gone from every commit on this branch — history rewritten and force-pushed, verified zero occurrences on the remote, `main` never affected.

**Not closed:** GitHub still serves the pre-rewrite commit at its SHA, confirmed through the API. That needs a Support garbage-collection request from someone with repo admin.

`scripts/check_no_real_pii.py` now blocks the class at commit time and in CI. Replaying the original incident against it is refused in the file where it first slipped through.

### The topics report, and the Pulse

The subject rooms are now split `topic` vs `software` — a subject the community discusses versus one named piece of software you install — and rendered one table per kind, topics first, each room carrying three tri-state flags. **"?" is not "no"**: a scan that hit its cap is unmeasured, and the cap is hit by *busy* rooms.

`aaif-community-pulse` now drafts one post per audience (organizers / `#general` / public), because the organizer post was being cross-posted verbatim to a room that reads channel renames and sheet changes as noise. `write_drafts.py` refuses the whole run if any draft carries an email or phone number.

## Test plan

- `PYTHONPATH=lib python -m pytest lib/aaif_events/tests -q` — 392 passed
- every `skills/*/scripts/test_*.py` and `scripts/test_*.py` — pass
- **with `gws` absent from `PATH`** — pass. Two suites reached the real CLI, so they passed locally and failed in CI, which has neither it nor credentials. CI was red for two runs before this.
- `pre-commit --all-files` — pass (now including `check-no-real-pii`)
- Live: gmail fallback verified against two real accounts; 188 ids + 188 Slack emails + 192 Drive emails written and read back. Full Slack audit re-run end to end against the fixed code.
